terms.gloss: a cleaner; here, the man who takes away the rubbish
terms.comment: From pūrgāre, to clean, as pūrgāmenta (rubbish) is; Apuleius and Firmicus have the word, Firmicus of a man who cleans the sewers. For the rubbish collector the use is ours. Levi–Bini give scōpārius, a sweeper, which Lewis & Short finds only once, in the Digest. The lorry is plaustrum pūrgāmentōrum or vehiculum pūrgāmentārium: descriptions of ours.

phrases.english: Can you hear? The dustmen are here: they’re taking the rubbish away.

phrases.latin: Crās māne pūrgātōrēs venient; excipula forās effer.
phrases.english: The dustmen are coming tomorrow morning; take the bins out.

sources: Lewis & Short: purgator · Lewis & Short: scoparius
Enrico Levi and Arturo Bini, Il latino come lingua viva (1937), p. 63, s.v. spazzaturaio.
